client: I've been really struggling since I graduated last May because I still haven't found a job in my field, and it's starting to feel like maybe I'm just not good enough. Everyone I went to school with seems to be posting about their new positions and careers on LinkedIn, and I can't even get a callback. Honestly, I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help, and I want you to know that what you're feeling — that creeping sense of "maybe I'm just not enough" — is such a painful place to sit, especially when it feels like everyone around you is moving forward. That thought, though, is worth gently examining together, because the job market being difficult isn't really the same thing as *you* being not good enough, even though our minds can blur those two things together. What do you think has been the loudest piece of evidence your mind keeps using to convince you that *you're* the problem, rather than the circumstances?

client: I guess the loudest thing my mind keeps throwing at me is that my friends from college all seem to have landed these solid jobs, like they figured it out and I'm still just... stuck. Every time I see someone post about a promotion or a new position, this voice in my head goes "see, it's you, you're the one who can't get it together." I hear what you're saying about circumstances versus me being the problem, but honestly it's hard to separate those two things when the rejection keeps feeling so personal.
therapist: That voice that says "see, it's you" is so convincing, especially when the pain of rejection keeps feeding it — and I really hear how exhausting it is to carry that comparison every time you open LinkedIn. One thing worth noticing is that you're essentially using other people's highlight reels as evidence about your own worth, when in reality you're only seeing their wins, not their struggles, rejections, or the luck involved in their timing. If a close friend came to you in your exact situation — same field, same market, same timeline — would that voice in your head tell *them* that they just "can't get it together"?

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them the job market is brutal right now and that it doesn't mean anything about who they are. But it feels different when it's me — like, I know all the ways I've fallen short, all the times I hesitated or didn't follow through, so the voice feels more... credible, I guess.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you just noticed that gap — you'd offer your friend compassion and context, but you hold yourself to a completely different standard, armed with every private doubt and misstep that nobody else sees. That "credibility" the voice has comes partly from the fact that you have *access* to your own hesitations in a way you simply don't have with your friends — but having more information about yourself doesn't automatically make the harshest interpretation the most accurate one. I'm curious — when you think about those moments you hesitated or didn't follow through, what do you think was actually going on for you then?

client: I guess... when I think about those moments, a lot of times I was just exhausted or overwhelmed, and I told myself I'd do it later but then later never came. But the voice in my head doesn't frame it that way — it just says I'm lazy or I don't care enough, and honestly that interpretation feels more true even when I try to push back against it. I think part of me is scared that if I let myself off the hook, I'll just keep not following through and confirm that the harsh voice was right all along.
therapist: What you just said is really insightful — you're essentially keeping the harsh voice in charge because you believe it's the thing protecting you from falling apart, but there's an important difference between self-compassion and letting yourself off the hook entirely. Recognizing that you were exhausted and overwhelmed isn't making excuses, it's actually *accurate information* that could help you understand what you need to follow through better — whereas "I'm lazy" just shames you without giving you anything useful to work with. What do you think might actually help you take action in those overwhelmed moments — not the harsh voice's answer, but what you, as someone who just showed a lot of self-awareness, genuinely thinks?

client: I mean... honestly, when I'm that overwhelmed, what probably would help is just breaking it down into something smaller, like not "clean the whole apartment" but just "put these three things away." But even as I say that, part of me is like, okay but I've told myself that before and I still didn't do it, so maybe I really am just lazy and the smaller steps thing is just another excuse I'm using. I guess I don't fully trust that being kinder to myself will actually change anything, because the harsh voice has been there so long it feels like it's the only thing that's ever gotten me to do anything at all.
therapist: You actually just identified something really practical and grounded — breaking things down — and then immediately the harsh voice swooped in to discredit it, which tells me that voice is very practiced at shutting down your own good instincts. It's worth asking though: if the harsh voice has truly been your engine all this time, how come it hasn't solved the procrastination problem yet — because a tool that was really working wouldn't still leave you feeling this stuck. What if the voice isn't actually what gets you moving, but rather what you've *survived despite*?

client: That actually... hit different, I have to admit. Like, I never thought about it that way — that maybe the harsh voice isn't driving me forward, it's just been something I've been dragging along with me this whole time. But it's hard to fully believe that, because if I let go of it, what's even left to push me?
therapist: That question — "what's left to push me?" — is such an important one, and I think it reveals that somewhere along the way you learned that you needed a threat to motivate you, rather than something you actually *want* to move toward. But you've been sitting here today, reflecting honestly, pushing back on hard ideas, showing up even when you doubted it would help — none of that was driven by the harsh voice, that was just *you*. So I'm curious: when you think about your field, the work you actually studied for — is there anything there that used to genuinely excite you, before all of this got so heavy?

client: I mean... yeah, there was a time when I actually loved the research side of things. I'd stay late in the lab not because I had to, but because I genuinely wanted to figure something out, like the problem itself was pulling me in. But honestly, it feels so far away now that I'm not even sure if that was real or if I've just built it up in my memory because everything now feels so bleak by comparison.
therapist: That memory of staying late in the lab — not because you had to, but because the problem was *pulling you in* — that's not something you invent, that's a real and specific feeling that bland nostalgia doesn't usually produce. The fact that it feels distant right now makes sense, because when we're worn down and discouraged for long enough, genuine passion can go quiet without disappearing entirely. What do you think that version of you — the one who stayed late because they *wanted* to — would think about the job search if they were the one leading it, rather than the harsh voice?

client: I sat with that for a second, and honestly... I think that version of me would probably be more curious about the search, like treating it as a puzzle to figure out rather than a test I'm already failing. But it's hard to access that right now because the rejections have kind of piled up and made everything feel like evidence that I was wrong about myself all along. I guess what I'm wondering is, how do I actually get back to that headspace when the discouragement feels so loud?
therapist: That reframe — from "test I'm already failing" to "puzzle to figure out" — is genuinely significant, and the fact that you could access it even briefly tells me that version of you isn't gone, just buried under a lot of accumulated pain. Getting back to that headspace probably isn't one big shift but small, deliberate moments of borrowing that curious perspective — even just for one small task — before the harsh voice has time to weigh in. What's one tiny piece of the job search that you could approach this week as an experiment to figure out rather than a verdict to survive?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible. But honestly, when I think about picking even one small thing from the job search, my mind immediately jumps to "what if I do it wrong" or "what's the point if nothing comes of it anyway." Maybe I could try rewriting just one section of my resume and tell myself I'm just experimenting with the wording rather than making it perfect, but I'm already bracing for that critical voice to show up the second I open the document.
therapist: It's really meaningful that even while anticipating the critical voice, you still landed on something concrete and genuinely workable — "experimenting with the wording" is exactly the kind of framing that belongs to that curious, lab-staying version of you, not the harsh voice. The critical voice showing up when you open the document isn't a sign that you're failing the experiment, it's just noise that you can notice and name — something like "there's that voice again" — without letting it be the judge of whether you keep going. What do you think it would feel like to finish that one small experiment, even imperfectly, just to prove to yourself that you can do it *with* the noise rather than only if it goes away first?

client: Honestly, that framing is kind of interesting — "with the noise rather than only if it goes away first." I think part of me has been waiting for the anxiety to just disappear before I let myself try, like I need perfect conditions to even start. But I'm not sure I fully trust that I can actually tolerate the discomfort in the moment — it's one thing to talk about it here and another to be sitting alone at my desk with that voice getting loud.
therapist: You've just named something really profound — that you've been waiting for perfect conditions that were never going to arrive, and there's something quietly hopeful in the fact that you can see that pattern so clearly now. The gap between talking about it here and sitting alone at your desk is real, and we're not pretending otherwise — but tolerating discomfort doesn't mean the voice goes quiet, it means you act for even just five minutes while it's loud and discover that you survived it. When that voice gets loud at your desk, what's one thing you could say to yourself in that moment — maybe something you'd tell that friend we talked about earlier — to help you stay in the experiment just a little longer?
